I am currently testing Dell's 32-inch UltraSharp U3226Q, and so far the experience has been very positive. With HDR enabled in macOS, the image quality on this OLED display is absolutely stunning. I will be posting a full review video of the UltraSharp on my YouTube channel later.

I also want to mention an important improvement to HDR support in macOS 27. When using an HDR-capable third-party display with macOS 26 Tahoe, one drawback was that you couldn't enable HDR with the common 2560 x 1440 scaled resolution. Fortunately, the latest version of macOS has resolved this issue.

The Problem

If you are using a third-party HDR10-capable display with macOS Tahoe, you will see a "High Dynamic Range" toggle in Settings → Displays. Once enabled, you can view HDR content. The image below shows an example.

But note that in the same screenshot, I have set the display resolution to 1920 x 1080, which is exactly the result of doubling the pixels from this 4K UHD display's native 3840 x 2160 resolution.

Most users probably wouldn't want to use 1920 x 1080, since content would appear too large on a 4K screen. The Dell UltraSharp U3226Q is a 32-inch display, so using 1920 x 1080 would significantly reduce the usable screen space.

Fixing this on macOS is simple—just choose a scaled resolution, such as the very common 2560 x 1440, which is also the default for Apple's 5K Studio Display. The problem is that in macOS Tahoe, selecting a scaled resolution disables HDR. See the screenshot below:

You can see that the "High Dynamic Range" toggle has disappeared, and macOS automatically switches back to SDR. In other words, if you're using macOS Tahoe with an HDR display, you must choose between HDR and your preferred scaled resolution.

Fortunately, this issue has been fixed in macOS 27 Golden Gate. As you can see in the screenshot below, scaled resolution and HDR can now be enabled simultaneously. This is a built-in system option—no third-party software required.

So if you're using a third-party HDR display, I think this feature alone is reason enough to upgrade from macOS Tahoe to macOS Golden Gate. Of course, what I'm testing here is an M4 MacBook Pro. I also tried the same scenario on an M1 Max MacBook Pro, and even running macOS 27, it couldn't select both settings at the same time—so it appears that hardware support is also required.

macOS Golden Gate introduces a host of new capabilities, which I've covered in my Siri AI overview, my macOS highlights video, and my macOS 27 roundup. One feature related to HDR displays is that macOS 27 provides more comprehensive native HDR support across the entire system.

You'll notice that highlights—especially spectral highlights, the cursor, and overall contrast—are noticeably better than in macOS Tahoe, making for a more striking viewing experience whether you're using an Apple Studio Display XDR, Pro Display XDR, or a third-party OLED display.

What do you think? Are you using a third-party external display with your Mac? If so, would you consider using an HDR-capable display?
